extracted.intended_audience: students of political philosophy and readers of Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for founding an ideal city: selection and education of guardian-soldiers, division of labor, and censorship/approval of stories and poetry used in early education. The passage prescribes moral, pedagogical, and theological standards for shaping citizens' character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: One man cannot practise many arts with success; each person should be assigned one work for which he is by nature fitted and at that should continue all his life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization ensures quality of workmanship and efficiency. From specialization follows the need for merchants, sailors, retail-traders, hirelings, etc., and the institutions (market-place, money) to facilitate exchange. Example reasoning: a shoemaker should not also be a husbandman if shoes are to be well made.

rubrics_metrics.name: War as an art requiring full-time practice
rubrics_metrics.description: War is an art requiring as much attention as shoemaking; a soldier cannot be a husbandman or artisan and be an effective warrior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mastery requires lifelong devotion, the city must cultivate a distinct military class (guardians) trained exclusively for defence and warfare rather than expecting part-time warriors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical qualities required of guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be quick to see, swift to overtake the enemy, and strong to fight when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy given to a well-bred dog: alertness, speed and strength are bodily attributes to be sought. These are necessary to perform the duties of defence effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological qualities of guardians (spirit and gentleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must possess spirit (thumos) — bravery and fierceness toward enemies — yet be gentle to friends and familiars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The apparent contradiction (spirited yet gentle) is resolved by analogy to animals (dogs) that distinguish friend from foe by knowledge; the desirable guardian combines spirited courage with controlled gentleness toward comrades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians should have philosophical/nascent-philosopher dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A really good guardian should unite philosophy (love of learning/wisdom) with spirit, swiftness and strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical traits make guardians able to distinguish friend from foe by knowledge; selection and education should aim to develop both intellectual and spirited qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of natures fitted for guarding
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the founders to select, if possible, natures which are fitted for the task of guarding the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is difficult and must be undertaken bravely and carefully; natural aptitude is necessary in addition to training, so screening of youth for appropriate dispositions is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of education: music (literature) before gymnastics
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should begin with music (inclusive of literature) before gymnastic training for the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children first hear tales (music/literature) at an age before physical training; the beginning is most important because early impressions are indelible and form character, so moral and intellectual content precedes physical conditioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and authorization of tales for the young
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a censorship of the writers of fiction: censors should receive any tale of fiction which is good and reject the bad; mothers and nurses must tell children the authorised tales only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ideas taken in early are indelible, the guardians of education must proactively shape the narrative environment of children. The founders set general forms in which poets should cast their tales, though founders need not compose the tales themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit erroneous representations of gods and heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: No erroneous representation is to be made of the nature of gods and heroes; tales that portray gods committing immoral acts or that present bad lies about the gods must be discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to exclude: Hesiod's account of Uranus and Cronus, tales that excuse or celebrate patricide or wicked behaviour by appealing to divine precedent. Such stories are unfit for the young because they may justify vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological principle: God is cause of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God is not the author of all things, but of good only; poets and reciters must represent the gods as truly good, as causes of goods, not of evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetic lines that attribute the dispensing of both good and evil to Zeus or that assert gods plant guilt among men. If poets recount punishments, they must frame them as just and ultimately beneficial to the punished, not as divine authorship of evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit depictions of gods as shape-changing or deceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not represent gods as magicians who change shape or deceive mankind; gods being perfect do not change themselves or willingly lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude myths of Proteus/Thetis disguises or any tale in which gods take on the likeness of strangers or use deception. The divine should be shown as immutable and truthful to cultivate proper reverence and morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress terrifying portrayals of the afterlife for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Expunge terrifying descriptions of the world below (Cocytus, Styx, sapless shades, etc.) that would make the young fear death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because guardians must be fearless of death, avoid songs and passages that produce excitable, effeminate nerves or fear of the underworld. Replace with nobler strains that do not render death dreadful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid lamentation and excessive mourning among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should not be given to weeping and wailing; they should not be represented as overwhelmed by sorrow at loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The good man is sufficient for himself and bears loss with equanimity; public education should model restraint — lamentations can be assigned to others so guardians scorn such displays and maintain courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit representations of guardians (and gods) overcome by laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of worth, and especially gods, must not be represented as overcome by laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive laughter produces a violent reaction and is unbecoming for worthy persons; omit poetic passages that depict even the gods indulging such laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of truth and restricted use of lies (noble lie for rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth should be highly valued; lying is only like a medicine and its use must be restricted. Rulers may be permitted to lie for the public good, but private individuals who lie should be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lies are useful only in limited cases (dealing with enemies, preventing harm) and should be the province of those trained to use them (rulers). Allowing lying generally undermines the State; punish craftsmen, priests, physicians, etc., who introduce lying practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as obedience and self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance consists chiefly of obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approve cultural materials (lines from epic) that model silent obedience and respect for leaders, and disapprove impertinent or mocking expressions toward rulers. Cultivate obedience and restraint in youth as elements of temperance.
